chief_complaint: sudden sharp ear pain, bleeding, and whistling sound when blowing nose after an open-hand slap directly to the ear
hpi_details: 31M assaulted with open-hand slap to left ear presenting with acute conductive hearing loss, tinnitus, and otoscopy confirming a clean, central 3 mm perforation of the pars tensa managed expectantly with strict water precautions and spontaneous healing over 4 weeks.
ideas: He thinks the sudden pressure from the slap burst a blood vessel and ripped a hole in his eardrum.
concerns: He is worried that the whistling noise and muffled sound mean his hearing has been permanently destroyed and will affect his ability to work.
expectations: He hopes the doctor will inspect the damage, confirm whether the eardrum will heal on its own, and provide ear drops to prevent an infection.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Traumatic Tympanic Membrane Perforation evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Traumatic Tympanic Membrane Perforation is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management follows an evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: sudden sharp ear pain, bleeding, and whistling sound when blowing nose after an open-hand slap directly to the ear

Key HPI features: 31M assaulted with open-hand slap to left ear presenting with acute conductive hearing loss, tinnitus, and otoscopy confirming a clean, central 3 mm perforation of the pars tensa managed expectantly with strict water precautions and spontaneous healing over 4 weeks.
Objective/Exam findings: Vital signs stable. Otoscopy shows a clean, central 3 mm perforation of the left pars tensa; no vertigo or facial weakness on exam.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Traumatic Tympanic Membrane Perforation.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Otitis media with perforation without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe vertigo or facial weakness — would suggest a more extensive injury beyond a simple perforation.
management_principles: Keep the ear dry and avoid instrumentation; most small clean traumatic perforations heal spontaneously, while vertigo, facial weakness, severe hearing loss, or persistent perforation requires urgent ENT assessment
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with sudden sharp ear pain, bleeding, and a whistling sound when blowing his nose after an open-hand slap directly to the ear. 31M assaulted with an open-hand slap to the left ear, now reporting acute conductive hearing loss and tinnitus.
reference_soap.objective: Vital signs stable. Otoscopy confirms a clean, central 3 mm perforation of the left pars tensa; no vertigo or facial weakness.
reference_soap.assessment: Traumatic tympanic membrane perforation, left ear, confirmed by otoscopy.
reference_soap.plan: Document otoscopic findings and hearing symptoms, keep the ear dry, and avoid ear drops or instrumentation unless specifically indicated. Most small clean traumatic perforations heal spontaneously; arrange audiometry/ENT follow-up. Seek urgent ENT assessment for vertigo, facial weakness, severe sensorineural hearing loss, contaminated injury, or a perforation that does not heal.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Perforation of Tympanic Membrane Traumatic Slap

Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for otolaryngology (ent)
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: A sudden pressure change from a slap to the ear tears the eardrum, causing sharp pain, some bleeding, and hearing changes — most small, clean perforations heal spontaneously with water precautions alone.
differentials: Skull base fracture (if more severe trauma)
red_flags: Severe vertigo or facial weakness — would suggest a more extensive injury beyond a simple perforation

must_ask.say: Can you describe exactly what happened to your ear?
How severe was the pain, and did you have any bleeding?
Has your hearing changed since the injury?
Do you notice air or a whistling sound when you blow your nose?
Any dizziness or ringing in your ear?

history.answer: I got slapped across the left side of my face earlier today, and now my left ear hurts, bled a little, and feels muffled.
It happened about four hours ago today, and all of the trouble is in my left ear.
Right when I was struck there was a sudden, sharp pain, but now it has settled into a dull ache around 3 out of 10. It does not get worse at night.
No, pulling on my earlobe or pressing in front of my ear does not hurt, and chewing feels totally fine.
I noticed a couple of drops of fresh red blood on a tissue right after the blow, but there is no yellow pus or foul smell.
Yes, right after the hit my left ear felt completely blocked and muffled, like it was stuffed with cotton.
There has been a persistent high-pitched ringing in my left ear, but the room is not spinning and I have zero dizziness.
Yes, when I blew my nose a short while ago, I heard and felt a whistling puff of air escaping through my left ear.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, or sweating.
No, I have not had a runny nose, stuffy nose, cough, or sore throat lately.
No, my face moves normally on both sides, and there are no blisters or sores around my ear or inside it.
No, there is no swelling or tenderness behind my ear, and I do not have a headache or a stiff neck.
No, I have not been swimming, have not showered since the incident, and have not put any cotton swabs or ear picks into my ear canal.
I was assaulted earlier today and struck with an open-hand slap directly over my left ear. Nothing was poked into the ear canal.
No, I have not flown on a plane or been scuba diving recently.
No, I do not have any tooth pain, jaw clicking, or habit of grinding my teeth.
No, my throat feels fine, swallowing is normal, my voice has not changed, and there are no bumps in my neck.
No, I have never had ear infections as an adult, no prior burst eardrums, and no ear surgeries.
No, I do not have diabetes or any condition affecting my immune system.
I think the hard slap popped my eardrum and tore something open inside.
I'm really worried this whistling means my ear is permanently ruined and I won't be able to hear properly on the job.
I do not have any chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter pain relievers, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used nicotine products.
I only drink an occasional beer on social occasions, maybe once or twice a month.

No one in my family has a history of hearing loss or chronic ear disorders.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.7 deg C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, comfortable young male in no acute distress, with faint erythema on the left cheek.
Left external auditory canal has a small streak of dried blood and a clean, central 3 mm perforation of the pars tensa; right ear is normal, with no pinna or mastoid tenderness bilaterally.
Weber test lateralizes to the left ear; Rinne test demonstrates bone conduction greater than air conduction on the left, and normal air conduction greater than bone conduction on the right.
Facial nerve motor function is fully intact with symmetric forehead wrinkling, eye closure, and smiling bilaterally.
No spontaneous or gaze-evoked nystagmus, and head impulse test is normal bilaterally.
Nasal passages are clear, and oral cavity, dentition, and pharynx show no lesions, swelling, or mucosal erythema.
Temporomandibular joints have full range of motion without clicking, pain, or crepitus bilaterally.
No preauricular, postauricular, or cervical lymphadenopathy palpable.
